title: The Value of Stories in Business | Aswath Damodaran | Talks at Google
description:
The world of investing/finance is divided into two camps. In one, you have the number-crunchers, who believe that the only things that matter are the numbers and that imagination/creativity are dangerous distractions. In the other, you have the storytellers, who build on the stories they tell about companies and how these stories will bring untold wealth. Each side believes it has a monopoly on the truth and looks with contempt at the other. Prof. Damodaran contends that stories matter, but only if they are connected with numbers. And numbers are empty, unless they are connected with narratives. In this talk, he looks at the process by which one might build narratives, check them against reality and convert them into valuations. Uber and Ferrari examples are used to illustrate the process.

Slides for the talk: https://goo.gl/zKVaQL

Check out the book on Google Play: https://goo.gl/tnGlDe

This talk was moderated by Saurabh Madaan.
summary: The speaker argues that consistent storytelling and a trusted narrative are critical for sustaining high valuations, citing Amazon as a prime example of a company that rewards the market with a high market cap despite lacking immediate profits. Conversely, the talk uses Valeant Pharmaceuticals as a cautionary tale of how a lack of trust and reputation damage can cause a company to unravel, regardless of its initial success. The discussion also highlights the importance of rigorous valuation models that account for necessary capital investments and operational realities, noting that simplistic growth assumptions often lead to incorrect conclusions.

claims.claim: Amazon's consistent story of prioritizing revenue and building a addicted consumer base explains its high valuation, as the market trusts a company that acts consistently with its long-term narrative.
claims.quote: He said, at Amazon we're going to go for revenues first and then after we've built the revenues, they will come, the profits. That's the story told in '97 and he's told the same story for 20 years. And he's acted consistently with that story. You know what I mean by acted consistently? How many people here have Amazon Prime? What do you pay for it? $99. Do you know what it costs Amazon to service every Prime member? About $400.
claims.speaker: ASWATH DAMODARAN

claims.claim: Amazon is building a business where it will eventually dominate by creating a consumer base addicted to its ecosystem, making it difficult for newcomers to enter the market.
claims.quote: What is he building with Amazon Prime? He's building this block of consumers who are addicted to Amazon, for lack of a better word, Who don't even know what a retail store looks like anymore. And one of these days, he's coming for you. So don't be surprised if a third nine pops up after the first two nines and you have nothing you can do, because where are you going to go? Everything else will be out of business by then.
claims.speaker: ASWATH DAMODARAN

claims.claim: Amazon serves as a perfect counter-example showing that if a company tells a consistent story over decades, the market will reward it with a high market cap even without immediate profits.
claims.quote: To me Amazon is the perfect counter-example of if you can tell a consistent story, markets will cut you a heck of a lot of slack. You know why they don't do it for most companies? Because the story keeps changing every year. The top management is incapable of telling the same story over time and then the market says, we don't trust you.
claims.speaker: ASWATH DAMODARAN

claims.claim: Valeant is described as a horror story and a reverse Cinderella story where a company fell from grace, starting in a castle and ending up cleaning chimneys, serving as a fascinating case study for behavioral and psychological issues in valuations.
claims.quote: I've been telling the story about Valeant for the last two years of a company that fell from grace, right? It's a reverse Cinderella story. It starts off with this-- you start off in the castle, you end up cleaning the chimneys. And I think it's fascinating sometimes watching horror stories unfold because you can see the behavioral and the psychological issues that play into these valuations.
claims.speaker: ASWATH DAMODARAN

claims.claim: Valeant unraveled when it got too ambitious and bought Salix, an $18 billion company, and tried to raise drug prices, causing the whole company to drop from $200 down to $32.
claims.quote: They got too ambitious. They got too big. They bought Salix, an $18 billion company. When they tried to raise the price of the drugs, people noticed. And the minute that happened, the whole company unraveled. It dropped from $200 down to $32. And I bought it at $32 saying, look, there's still enough value in the company.
claims.speaker: ASWATH DAMODARAN

claims.claim: Valeant did so much damage to its reputation that nobody trusted them, making it impossible to build an R&D department or hire scientists, which prevented the company from becoming an old-fashioned drug company.
claims.quote: You know what I missed is this company did so much damage to its reputation. We talk about corporate sustainability. It taught me a lesson about why corporate sustainability has a place in Valeant. They had done so much damage to their reputation that nobody trusted them. Because I assumed that they would become an old fashioned drug company. But to become an old fashioned drug company, what do you have to do? You have to build an R&D department, you've got to hire scientists.
claims.speaker: ASWATH DAMODARAN

claims.claim: Valeant's attempt to sell a portion of its business failed because potential buyers viewed the company as liars and did not trust them, highlighting the importance of corporate sustainability.
claims.quote: They try to sell a portion of the business. I'm Valeant, I try to sell a portion of my business to you. What's your reaction? You guys are liars. I don't trust anythin
claims.speaker: ASWATH DAMODARAN

claims.claim: The speaker describes Uber as a ride-sharing service that acts as a matchmaker, collecting 20% of fares while drivers keep 80%, and notes that drivers use it to earn a second income legally.
claims.quote: She said, it's a ride-sharing service. I said, what the heck is a ride-sharing service? She said, I don't have the time to tell you. Why don't you just download the app and find out for yourself? So I hang up the phone, I download the app, and I hit the app.
claims.speaker: Aswath Damodaran

claims.claim: The speaker explains that Uber drivers are independent contractors who use the platform to pick up passengers legally, earning 80% of the fare while Uber takes a 20% commission.
claims.quote: He said, I'm an independent contractor. I said, why do you do this? He says, I have a regular job. I don't make enough money and this allows me to make a second income in a car that I already own.
claims.speaker: Aswath Damodaran

claims.claim: The speaker notes that Uber drivers do not pay extra insurance because they rely on their existing coverage, and Uber collects 20% of the fare while sending 80% to the driver.
claims.quote: He said, I don't mention it to the insurance company. What they don't know, they don't know. So basically, he was taking the car, he was using the insurance he already had and making a second income and Uber was the matchmaker that allowed him to do it.
claims.speaker: Aswath Damodaran

claims.claim: The speaker mentions that Ferrari was spun off as an independent company in 2015 after Enzo Ferrari sold 90% of the company to Fiat Chrysler in the 1960s.
claims.quote: But in the 1960s, Enzo Ferrari got into some trouble and he had to sell off 90% of Ferrari to Fiat Chrysler and for about 50 years, Ferrari stayed as a part of Fiat Chrysler, until 2015 when it was spun off as an independent company.
claims.speaker: Aswath Damodaran

claims.claim: The speaker criticizes a valuation model for Tesla that assumes high growth without accounting for necessary capital investment in new plants.
claims.quote: In fact, I called the analyst and I pushed him on it and he admitted finally that it had slipped his mind. I made a suggestion to him. I said, you know what? The only way you're going to be able to get away with this is you need to watch "Willy Wonka's Chocolate Factory."
claims.speaker: Aswath Damodaran

claims.claim: The speaker explains that his valuation model assumed Uber would never buy cars or hire drivers, allowing for easy growth.
claims.quote: And finally, I also assumed that they would never buy the cars, they would never hire the drivers, which means that they can grow relatively easily. So the way I reflected that is for every dollar they invested, they got $5 of revenues.
claims.speaker: Aswath Damodaran

claims.claim: The speaker notes that Tech Crunch readers hated his valuation of Uber, feeling it was inappropriate for a Silicon Valley company.
claims.quote: The Tech Crunch people absolutely hated it. They said, how dare you value one of ours with your d.c.f. We don't do that in Silicon Valley. I got this wave of abuse.
claims.speaker: Aswath Damodaran

claims.claim: The speaker mentions receiving an email from Bill Gurley who wrote a counter-post to his Uber valuation.
claims.quote: And finally, from the Ride-Sharing Guy, I had some very interesting things about the 80-20 mix. They said, this is unusual. Uber doesn't get to keep 20% because they kick it back. They pay us $1,500 to switch from Lyft.
claims.speaker: Aswath Damodaran

claims.claim: The speaker explains that Uber's 80-20 revenue mix was unusual because they pay drivers $1,500 to switch from Lyft, contradicting their public claims.
claims.quote: They said, this is unusual. Uber doesn't get to keep 20% because they kick it back. They pay us $1,500 to switch from Lyft. And I would never have found this out by talking to Uber's top management, right? Because they want to preserve the illusion for the investors of its 20%.
claims.speaker: Aswath Damodaran

claims.claim: The speaker points out a discrepancy where Uber claimed to keep 20% of revenue while losing $4 billion on $6 billion revenue.
claims.quote: They said, we're still keeping 20%. Then how the heck are you losing $4 billion on a $6 billion revenue? The numbers don't gel, right?
claims.speaker: Aswath Damodaran

claims.claim: The speaker describes receiving an email from Bill Gurley who wrote a counter-post to his Uber valuation.
claims.quote: And finally, from the Ride-Sharing Guy, I had some very interesting things about the 80-20 mix. They said, this is unusual. Uber doesn't get to keep 20% because they kick it back. They pay us $1,500 to switch from Lyft.
claims.speaker: Aswath Damodaran

claims.claim: The speaker notes that Bill Gurley wrote a counter-post to his Uber valuation after reading his blog post.
claims.quote: And finally, from the Ride-Sharing Guy, I had some very interesting things about the 80-20 mix. They said, this is unusual. Uber doesn't get to keep 20% because they kick it back. They pay us $1,500 to switch from Lyft.
claims.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
